pherical polyhedron can be mapped to a highly symmetrical space known as a hyperbolic triangle. This mapping maintains the distance between points according to the hyperbolic metric. The angle at each vertex of the triangle, however, is not necessarily 120 degrees as would be expected in a Euclidean space. Rather, the angles are determined by the hyperbolic metric at those vertices. This paper explores the relationship between the hyperbolic triangle and the spine of the polyhedron. It establishes that the hyperbolic triangle represents the geometric essence of the spine. As a result, any transformation of the hyperbolic triangle corresponds to a similar transformation of the spine. This relationship provides the basis for proving that the spine of the polyhedron is also aspherical.

Adversarial Networks (GANs) can effectively generate high-quality virtual spectra for various observational instruments.  Despite this, no study has yet applied these methods to the analysis of large spectroscopic surveys, aligning with the approach of Guo et al. (2020).  Extending that work, we introduce a novel architecture built upon the type of generator network used in Guo et al. (2020), with distinct sub-networks for producing line fluxes and widths.  This innovative design enhances the model's ability to replicate the WISE survey's spectral characteristics, particularly at regions with intense absorption.  Leveraging the strengths of both the traditional method of spectral synthesis and the Guo et al. (2020) approach, we introduce a two-step modeling process that first generates a coarse representation of the spectrum using a compact set of analysis lines, and then refines this output with an additional set of broad features.  This hybrid model demonstrates superior performance in mimicking the WISE survey's spectral features and is more versatile in creating realistic spectra across various stellar types.  Ultimately, this method holds significant potential for enhancing the analysis of large spectroscopic surveys and facilitating the incorporation of additional observational data.

researchers have been exploring various methods to enhance the capability of indoor localization systems. One such approach involves using the time-of-arrival and extreme values of signal strength from multiple access points to determine a device's location. In this research, we examine the effectiveness of using the extreme value of signal strength from a single access point for indoor localization. Our results show that using the minimum or maximum signal strength can lead to a significant reduction in the mean squared error in location estimation, up to a 75% reduction in certain scenarios. We attribute this improvement to the diverse nature of signal strength readings, with stronger readings indicating a device's proximity to an access point. Moreover, we found that using the extreme value of signal strength can greatly increase the accuracy of location estimation, especially in areas with strong line-of-sight to an access point.

A recent study of the AGN best practices for analyzing multi-wavelength light curves established a common framework for analysis with the use of discrete variable analysis.  Applying this method to a large sample of 424 quasars at high redshifts from the Giant Gemini Quasar Survey, we discovered a distinct population of intrinsically bright and short-timescale UV variables. This study introduces an innovative approach using Twitter and Wikipedia to examine the circulation and persistence of misinformation within an emerging event. We focus on the Wikipedia edit history of the event's related pages and analyze the Wikipedia references supported by Twitter tweets. By identifying the time it takes for these references to appear on Wikipedia and the subsequent editing history of those pages, we evaluate the information's persistence. We further develop a metric called information impact, defined as the product of the time it takes for the information to reach Wikipedia and the subsequent change made to the page, to compare different pieces of information. We apply our method to analyze the Wikipedia edit history of the Wikipedia references from Twitter tweets during the COVID-19 pandemic. The results show that Twitter tweets that lead to Wikipedia edits appear on the target Wikipedia page 3.5 days earlier if they are posted by influential users, have more retweets, or belong to a wider Twitter discussion. Additionally, Wikipedia pages with greater change persistence in terms of content and structure are those that were initially created to provide general information about the target entity, rather than those designed to provide comprehensive, in-depth information.

Implementing SPS using linear optical components is challenging due to the need for an almost perfect single-photon source. In this study, we propose utilizing a hot atomic ensemble, known for its high visibility atomic quantum nonlocality, as a near-perfect single-photon source in SPS. The proposed setup involves an atomic ensemble interacting with a weak coherent state in the context of quantum computing using spatial modes. The ability of the atomic ensemble to exhibit almost perfect single-photon generation, demonstrated through simulations, makes it a viable source for SPS. The model also allows for the reduction of cross-talk between different spatial modes, a feature that could contribute to complex quantum computations using spatial modes. The simplicity and reliability of the atomic ensemble also address the limitations of using linear optical components, and the system's low scattering rates could increase the success rate of SPS.

study a specific class of holographic tensor networks, namely the multi-qubit states based on quantum circuits, whose virtual degrees of freedom exhibit quasi-local properties.  By relating circuit states to corresponding holographic duals, we investigate the fundamental characteristics of this particular type of quasi-locality.  Our analysis reveals that for circuit states with a smooth, stable 'horizon', the quasi-local degrees of freedom behave similarly to those in holographic theories with smooth boundaries.  We also find that a particular notion of quasi-locality is directly related to the conformal symmetry present in the AdS space.  Building upon these findings, we explore the broader implications for quasi-local degrees of freedom in system-horizon setups.  We show that in cases where the horizon is unstable or interacting with the system's quasi-local degrees of freedom, situations that we term 'horizon dynamics', the quasi-local degrees of freedom can exhibit similar behavior to that observed in the AdS space.  These findings suggest that quasi-locality may provide a more fundamental characteristic underlying the horizon dynamics in systems such as those studied in black hole physics.

Originally developed in the 1980s and 1990s, the general formula for JPDA has been applied to various scenarios despite being mathematically complex.  For a single target with a known initial position, moving at a constant velocity, the probability of association is calculated as the product of local likelihood densities along an expected trajectory.  This paper presents an innovative approach to predicting the target's trajectory and local likelihood densities for a general JPDA algorithm.  By modeling the target's motion as a Gaussian process and deriving the Gaussian mixture representation of the JPDA algorithm, the researcher overcame previous limitations and successfully applied the method to unknown initial positions, resulting in a novel adaptive JPDA algorithm. two parts: the setup and the punchline.
  The primary function of a joke's setup is to establish a clear, concise understanding
  for the listener. In contrast, the punchline's purpose is to create unexpected
  semantic connections with the setup, often by employing various forms of wordplay.
  In this research, we propose an automated method to identify wordplay used in
  puns within a joke. Our approach is centered on creating a set of pre-defined
  semantic relationships that can be applied universally to all words in a language.
  We have collected a comprehensive dataset of 1000+ words in Russian and established
  a comprehensive list of 133 pre-defined semantic relationships, which can be
  extended to any Russian word. By utilizing these relationships, we have developed
  a fully automated system to pinpoint instances of wordplay in Russian puns with
  an accuracy of over 90%. Our research indicates that the vast majority of wordplay
  in Russian can be categorized into one of the 133 pre-defined relationships we
  have established, which suggests that a large percentage of a language's wordplay
  can be identified using a limited, universally applicable list of relationships.

message-locked scheme with non-degenerate sums is proposed for private message transmission. In this context, an encoder sorts users' secret messages in ascending order and assigns a coded symbol to each user, with the caveat that these coded symbols share the same average intensity as the original messages. A decoder, equipped with the summed signal, determines the ranking of all users' messages and identifies the message corresponding to the sum. Notably, the degree of privacy is directly tied to the degree of the sum, with higher-degree sums providing greater privacy at the cost of a decreased transmission rate. In theoretical calculations, the optimal transmission rates for achieving various degrees of privacy are determined, with the advantage of this scheme lying in its ability to protect users' message contents while only revealing the ranking of messages.  Simulation results in a wireless channel confirm the validity of these theoretical findings.

This particular pairing configuration is particularly prevalent in superconducting materials that exhibit o-wave pairing, specifically in the vicinity of high-Tc superconducting cuprates' copper oxidatic interfaces. This theoretical study explores the consequences of connecting this device to an external o-wave mesoscope, allowing the 2D o-wave condensate to be manipulated as a controlled non-equilibrium system. in unsupervised learning, extensively used for protecting sensitive information by releasing summaries of data instead. We investigate a specific type of clustering called $k$-means clustering, where the goal is to release a summary of cluster centers for $k$ non-parametric components, and the true data remains private. We establish an asymptotic analysis for the clustering error of the released centers, demonstrating that the optimal performance is achieved by a parametric component, and the remaining $k-1$ components can be seen as noise with a specific distribution. Additionally, we formulate a minimax lower bound for the clustering error, and this lower bound is essentially the same as the asymptotic optimal performance when there are only two non-parametric components. We also explore a specific distribution, the Gaussian mixture, and show that the asymptotic optimal performance can be attained under this distribution by a straightforward method. We further extend our results to a more general case where the true data consists of $K \geq k$ components, and we establish a cluster-wise minimax lower bound. This lower bound implies that improving the clustering error of the released centers from $\frac{K^2}{(K+k)(K-k)}$ when there are two components, to something closer to $K$ when there are many components, is essentially the same as resolving the mixture detection problem with a known number of components.

(OOD) data within conversational dialogue systems is a growing area of concern. These systems are regularly expected to process a wide range of information, and therefore, need to identify and respond appropriately to unfamiliar information. To address this issue, we propose a new dataset, called ConvOOD, which focuses on dialogue data. This dataset contains 8,162 dialogue labels from 152 topics, and is utilized in experiments to evaluate current methods' capabilities to detect in-domain and out-of-domain information within conversations. The results show that these methods perform significantly better when evaluating in-domain and out-of-domain information within isolated text segments; nevertheless, their performance suffers substantially when evaluating the same information within dialogue contexts. Notably, the difference in performance varies based on the domain and context in question. For instance, when evaluating scientific domains, the variation in performance is significantly more pronounced. To take this challenge further, we explore several methods to provide early warnings when encountering out-of-domain information and discover that incorporating a one-shot learning approach along with additional supporting evidence leads to more accurate early warnings. Furthermore, we introduce a simplified model that combines our proposed methods with established techniques to handle this challenge, and the results indicate that these methods can be successfully applied to out-of-domain detection within conversations.

  electron-screening effects. Calculating these effects requires accurate
  boundary conditions, namely the point of no return and the turning point,
  which are typically estimated using nuclear potential models. Conversely,
  electron-screening effects on radiative transitions are generally
  disregarded due to their minor influence. This study aims to rectify this
  oversight and evaluate the screening effects on radiative transitions in
  low-energy $\beta$ and $\beta$+$\gamma$ spectra. This will facilitate a
  more precise understanding of the screening effects in nuclear processes.
  Methodology: We derived a formula for the screening factor in the
  relativistic nuclear potential model and evaluated its impact on the
  calculated boundaries in low-energy $\beta$ and $\beta$+$\gamma$ spectra.
  Notably, we applied this approach to evaluate the screening effects on
  transition energies and spectra of $^{18}$F and $^{118}$Xe. The results
  were then contrasted with available experimental data and theoretical models.

  radiative transitions in low-energy $\beta$ and $\beta$+$\gamma$ spectra

In this study, we introduce a statistical framework for assessing the significance of these patterns, and apply it to a broad class of recurrent neural networks.   where the policy updates are performed entirely based on a pre-collected dataset 
  of state-action pairs.  Due to the lack of interactions with the environment, 
  the learned policy may not accurately reflect the underlying dynamics.  
  Recently, a type of offline reinforcement learning method has gained popularity, 
  where the objective is optimized directly through an expected long-term reward 
  estimate, but faces a significant challenge in resolving the representation learning 
  issue.  To address this, we propose a new offline reinforcement learning framework, 
  based on an unregularized maximum likelihood principle, that leverages a unique 
  state representation learning module.  This module extracts a compact latent 
  space from the original state space and the policy is learned with regards to 
  this representation.  We show that this framework allows the problem of 
  representation learning to be resolved and the challenge of entropy reduction 
  to be addressed by maximizing the marginal likelihood of the action probabilities.  
  By utilizing a differentiable latent function and action selection policy, 
  our framework can be optimized efficiently through the reversal of the 
  differentiable functions.  We validate the effectiveness of our framework 
  by applying it to both the policy-based and value-based offline reinforcement 
  learning scenarios and the results indicate that it consistently outperforms the 
  corresponding baseline methods.

United Nations has implemented multiple anti-piracy resolutions through its Security Council, urging states to suppress and prevent pirate activities.  Despite these efforts, pirate groups have persisted and adapted, posing a significant threat to global shipping lanes.  This research focuses on analyzing how states comply with these anti-piracy obligations and explores the underlying factors that influence this compliance.  A qualitative comparative analysis was conducted, examining 22 countries that have interacted with pirate groups at some point since 2000.  Our study leverages the Configurational Comparative Method, specifically the RQAGS package in R, to analyze the data.  We identified two key conditions that satisfy the Necessity and Sufficiency criteria among the 22 countries: a democratic system and involvement in naval operations.  In particular, we found that countries with a democratic system in place have consistently prioritized anti-piracy efforts, whereas states involved in naval operations have demonstrated a heightened sense of responsibility in addressing pirate activities.  Our study contributes to the literature by introducing the concept of "responsibility dynamics" to describe how states' attitudes towards international obligations evolve in response to changing circumstances.

Through experiments using diamonds containing uranium, we have demonstrated the possibility of simultaneously sensing magnetic fields and nuclear scintillations, including the scintillations generated by the decay of sodium-22, a major contributor in certain environments. This study complements that body of work by exploring the effects of noisy stock price data on a machine learning-based trading agent, particularly one that maximizes long-term portfolio value.  We established the existence of an optimal trading strategy in the presence of noisy market data, and our findings reveal that the level of noise has a non-decreasing impact on the performance of the trading agent, specifically causing it to engage in more frequent and dramatic trades. We further found that if the noise level meets certain criteria, the stationary component can be eliminated, and we were able to derive an explicit formula for the stationary component in certain cases of noise. explore the cosmos, examining bright active galactic nuclei in depth.  The high-energy phenomena of these objects are largely understood through the study of the gamma-ray energy band.  The formation of broad emission lines depends on the presence of high-energy flux, and when present, they can be extremely luminous.  These lines can also be used as a reference point to study the galaxy in which the active galactic nucleus resides.  As such, we analyze a comprehensive AGN sample from the SDSS, focusing on objects with emission lines that are bright and narrow, and we discuss how the line strength relates to other characteristics.  We find that the equivalent width of these lines is approximately 200 Angstroms, and the ratio of line to continuum flux can be as high as 10.  We also observe a direct relationship between the velocity of these lines and the perspective viewer, which we attribute to differential redshift.  This effect results in a 1000 km/s shift in the average line velocity as the line strength increases by a factor of 10.  This relationship can be understood through the interaction of a broad line that has shifted downwards and a narrow line that has shifted upwards.

time evolution of matter in a one-dimensional Young diamond, a semi-classical setup with mirror symmetry, using a quantum hydrodynamics approach. A nearly uniform quantum state is used as an initial condition and the quantum hydrodynamics equations are solved numerically to analyze the spreading of this state. A comparison is made with a classical hydrodynamics simulation which shows similar spreading patterns, providing a connection between quantum and classical chaos in this system. The quantum hydrodynamics approach also allows us to identify a specific signature of chaos, the emergence of a long tail in the spectrum of a quantum correlation function, which we refer to as a "quantum scarring". This "quantum scarring" appears in both the hydrodynamics simulation and a microscopically exact quantum simulation, indicating that it captures an essential feature of chaotic quantum dynamics. However, we find that in this system, "quantum scarring" requires a specific preparation of the initial quantum state, whereas in classical hydrodynamics, it occurs for any initial condition. Additionally, the "quantum scarring" in the spreading of a uniform state can be distinguished from an uniform spread by measuring a quantum correlation function in the momentum basis, which further highlights the utility of considering these quantities in the study of chaotic quantum systems.

, numerous implications arise due to the speed of light's constant velocity. One such consequence involves the theory's incompatibility with the possibility of superluminal communication, which can be understood through the formation of a "faster-than-light" channel that is actually a mathematical impossibility. To demonstrate this in a visual manner, we create a "win-loss" game involving two players. One player, the receiver, attempts to accurately reconstruct an encoded message sent by another, the sender, with the constraint that they cannot communicate at speeds greater than light. If the receiver successfully reconstructs the message, the sender incurs a loss, whereas the reverse holds true for unsuccessful attempts. Given that the speed of light's constancy allows for the definition of a well-determined "early-late" distinction in time differences, we posit that real, observable "win-loss" effects can be produced. To support this claim, we consider a scenario inspired by Einstein, where two individuals, the sender and receiver, move at right angles to each other at speeds close to the speed of light. We then show that, under these conditions, the "win-loss" phenomenon can be observed. Furthermore, we propose an experimental design using the "win-loss" game in conjunction with particle entanglement to demonstrate its feasibility. If observed, this experiment would provide empirical evidence for the speed of light's significance in communication.

The study employs an Ambrosi-Bonetti-type approach, introducing a conformal field that enables expression of the logarithmic divergence of the conformal field's energy density at the location of the vortices as a surface tension with an orientation determined by the conformal field's gradient. The study also investigates the conformal field's angular and linear (logarithmic) modes separately, establishing that the linear (logarithmic) mode represents the angular (linear) mode of an Einstein-Yang-Mills vortex line. To address this question, we design a novel attention-based position representation, denoted as T-Scale, to provide comprehensive analysis at multiple scales within the attention-based ViT framework. Moreover, our model achieves 18% cost reduction in parameter usage, 9% reduction in computation, 10% reduction in memory occupancy, 8% reduction in optimization steps

By analyzing the first and second observing runs, we examined how merger angles distribute among all detections.  We discovered the distribution is nearly uniform up to a certain angle limit ($\theta_{\rm lim} \approx 0.45$ rad) but becomes irregular beyond it.  Since no pattern emerges in the irregular zone, we assume a binary black hole merger angle is either fixed at $\theta_{\rm lim}$ or varies freely within that limit. Consequently, the detected objects tend to have more favorable signal-to-noise ratios when the distribution is uniform compared to a binary black hole merger angle being fixed at $\theta_{\rm lim}$.

, specifically the silicon pixel detector, was upgraded to enhance precision and stability in the measurement of track parameters and particle flow during LHC operations with higher luminosity levels.  A new design featuring a redesigned readout electronic circuit with reduced noise sensitivity and increased data transmission efficiency was implemented.  The modification replaces separate readout chips with an integrated design, using a single 40 MHz readout chip instead of four 1.8 GHz chips per 66 mm$^2 area.  This upgrade was completed in 2016 just before the start of LHC operation with an integrated luminosity of $25 \mathrm{~nb}^{-1}$.  To evaluate the performance of this upgrade, a comprehensive analysis of data collected with an integrated luminosity of $13 \mathrm{~pb}^{-1}$ is presented.  The results show a mean charge collection efficiency loss of $79.3\%$ in the most irradiated region of the detector, in accordance with predicted values, and a mean noise hit probability of $3.1\%$ for the most irradiated layer, lower than the $6.4\%$ estimate. The primary focus of these notes is on the application of algebraic methods to solve a specific type of exactly solvable Hamiltonian matrix that arises in one-dimensional scattering theory. Specifically, I explore the underlying structure of a particular Hamiltonian matrix that represents a scattering system with a finite number of interacting states, and I establish an important condition - which I call a'strong sign definiteness condition' - that ensures the eigenvalues of this Hamiltonian matrix are real and distinct, resulting in a unique and non-degenerate spectral transformation. In our results, we find that the new miner can successfully infiltrate the established player's protocol only if it is able to mine blocks at a rate at least equal to that of the established player. We also observe in our simulations that one of the established player strategies can successfully infiltrate the new miner's protocol even if it is able to mine blocks at a rate up to ten times that of the new miner.

, and neural networks rely on representations that capture relevant information to solve complex problems.  The rise of state-of-the-art models like Transformers has been rapid, yet the underlying mechanisms of these models, particularly in tasks dealing with structured inputs and outputs, is not well understood.  To address this, we present the Input-Output Linear Transformation (IOLT) model, a simple framework based on traditional neural network principles, and apply it to the task of machine translation.  By fracturing the embedding matrix into two components, one for input and one for output, the IOLT model can be seen as a form of factorization that eliminates the need for position embeddings and output linear transformations.  We find that IOLT representations perform on par with baseline Transformers, and our analysis reveals that the factors are closely related to the attention-based representations and output linear transformations of the baseline model.  What's more, the IOLT model is highly versatile, making it easily adaptable to other tasks such as summarization, and it does so without the need for task-specific modifications to the representation layer.  We believe that the success of the IOLT model marks an important step towards a deeper understanding of the mechanisms behind modern Transformers, and we hope this will inspire further research into the underlying mechanics of these models.

organisms and their characteristics are often determined by a specific set of atoms called functionally critical sites.  These sites are atoms that maintain a specific level of spatial proximity under normal conditions and at specific time intervals, and their identification is crucial for understanding how proteins interact with other molecules.  A method commonly used for detecting these critical sites relies on statistical averages to identify clusters of closely situated atoms; however, this method has limitations when dealing with dynamic protein structures.  In order to identify these critical sites in structures that are known about proteins, we developed a new method that avoids relying on statistical averages.  Instead of looking at instances of spatial proximity between atoms, this method focuses on the total number of instances in which certain atoms appear close to each other.  With the aim of identifying critical sites in the structures of membrane proteins, we applied our method to a dataset of non-viral membrane proteins and were able to pinpoint locations that are near passages of lipids in the cell membrane and areas that are difficult to access for the solvent.  Furthermore, we discovered certain critical sites that are shared between different proteins and are involved in various biological functions, and our results highlight the potential of this method to contribute to the advancement of protein analysis.

The Helmholtz decomposition is a fundamental concept used to express a vector field as a combination of a scalar potential and a gradient of a scalar function. In continuous systems with singular distributions, the traditional Helmholtz decomposition is not universally applicable and depends on the type of singularity. Despite its widespread use, EEG data continues to pose analysis challenges due to its high-dimensional nature and inherent noise.  Deep learning-based approaches have achieved notable success in interpreting EEG signals by providing automatic feature extraction, thus eliminating the need for time-consuming manual processes.  A key issue with these models is their limited generalizability across different datasets, which hinders real-world applications.  In an effort to address this problem, we've developed a novel neural network architecture called the Resonant Attention Recurrent Neural Network (RARNN).  This innovative model is designed to enhance EEG-based mental state prediction by incorporating an attention mechanism to compensate for the non-stationarity of EEG signals.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of RARNN through comparative studies on multilabel EEG data, which reinforces the benefits of using this model.  Interestingly, our findings indicate that RARNN performs equally well on datasets with and without RNN layers, which we attribute to the robustness of the attention mechanism.

Despite the progress made in the field of deep learning, the process of manual feature extraction remains unchanged, which hinders progress in certain areas of research.  One such area is the study of cardiac mechanics, which involves understanding how the heart moves and interacts with surrounding fluids.  Researchers in this field who use numerical methods to simulate the heart must first remove generated artificial cycles from realistic records of cardiac motion, a task that requires expert knowledge and manual feature extraction for high-quality results.  In this work, we develop a novel method using a form of recurrent neural networks called the encoder-decoder model that automatically extracts useful information and facilitates the removal of artificial cycles from real cardiac cycles. Court rulings provide a rich source of insights, given their basis in fundamental ethical principles and their influence on shaping and applying laws. This study focuses on court decisions related to social welfare, examining over 1.5 million US law documents from 1803 to present and utilizing over 300,000 modern decisions with annotated policies. We developed a technique to identify the underlying values represented in these documents, establishing a set of 200 primary principles that capture the essence of US social welfare laws. These principles allow us to gain new insights into the evolution of laws over time, statistics on the most influential concepts, and the relationship between laws and external factors such as economic conditions and philanthropic efforts. For example, we found that laws related to business, family, and international relations have experienced steady growth, whereas those concerning education have seen a significant surge in recent years; we also discovered that the 2008 financial crisis had a limited impact on these laws but sparked a renewed interest in business and finance.

The membrane's edge is assumed to remain rigid throughout the experiment. A specialized finite element method is used to analyze the elliptical membrane, with the program capable of adapting to various edge configurations and pressure variations. However, current approaches primarily concentrate on utilizing the reference image as a source of input and obscure its significance when the reference image is meant to provide an additional guidance input, similar to text descriptions. To address this limitation, our research focuses on developing a method that lets the reference image provide both input and guidance. To achieve this, we split the reference image into multiple smaller patches and train two separate networks: a patch-level network and a global network. ar graph structures that reflect the symmetry of a graph, encompassing the symmetry of its vertices. The isomorphism types of these structures hold significance in graph symmetry, particularly in determining whether a graph has a non-trivial symmetry. For a graph to have a non-trivial symmetry, its twin groups and virtual twin groups must have an isomorphism type that is non-trivial. In this research, we examine the application of virtual twin groups in identifying the non-trivial symmetry of graphs. We introduce the concept of a graph being "good", defined as having twin groups and virtual twin groups that are isomorphic to those of a cyclic group or a dihedral group, for any possible symmetry it may have. We then classify cyclic graphs, bipartite graphs, and directed graphs as to whether they are classified as "good" or not, based on their degree pattern. Specifically, we find that cyclic graphs with a non-trivial symmetry exist only if their vertex count is even, bipartite graphs with the same condition exist if the difference between the vertex counts in the two sets is either zero or a multiple of three, and directed graphs with the condition exist if their edge count is either zero or a multiple of three.

the Universe will eventually undergo a "Big Rip" catastrophe, where the expansion accelerates to the point of tearing apart all matter. Using an ensemble of simulated universes with varying cosmological parameters, we found that when the Big Rip occurs, it triggers a sudden surge in the production of primordial black holes, specifically those with masses in the range of millions to billions of times the mass of the Sun. These primordial black holes would form at roughly the same rate regardless of the specifics of the Universe's cosmology, producing an average of about 10^11 times the mass of the Sun per year. However, if the Universe experiences a prolonged period of inflation before the Big Rip, the primordial black holes with the highest masses would dominate the production rate, potentially leading to an exponential increase in their formation during this time. The formation of these primordial black holes could result in gravitational waves with distinctive characteristics, potentially detectable by next-generation gravitational wave observatories, and could also produce a cosmic gamma-ray burst in the Universe's early stages if they contribute significantly to the early cosmic gamma-ray background.

The theory involves a self-interacting scalar field with a self-consistent self-interaction, and we analyze the effects of an external field on the underlying symmetries that govern its behavior. The presence of an external field causes the theory's symmetry to break, resulting in an assembly of quasi-symmetric states that interact with each other. We observe that the presence of an external field leads to an alteration in the number of possible fixed points from two to none, except for the case where the scalar field's mass is zero. We also find that the Big Bang trajectory is always repelled by the stable fixed points, and that the stable fixed points correspond to an exponential decrease in the model's energy. We further find that the stable fixed points can be reached through an exponential decrease in the model's energy, and that the dominant quasi-symmetric state exhibits an algebraic decrease in the model's energy.

core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) occur at the end of high-mass star lives, making their linked phenomena, core-collapse GRBs (CCGRBs), of great interest for understanding these processes. We propose that the most massive stars can develop two critical physical limitations due to their finite angular momentum, leading to different outcomes based on their mass:  above a certain mass, stars collapse directly into black holes, while those below it can rotate rapidly and produce a jetted GRB.  If a star has sufficient mass to produce a massive outer envelope, it will instead give rise to a CCSNe.  This duality-based model can resolve many of the difficulties faced by other CCGRB theories and is supported by the characteristics of observed data, specifically the relative rates of long/short GRBs and types II/IIIP/X/IX CCGRBs.  However, the model also generates a prediction that can be verified with future observations:  the majority of CCGRBs are actually associated with CCSNe, which can be validated using newly compiled statistics on CCGRB-SNe associations and rates, along with the likelihood of additional uncompiled cases, totaling approximately 1-2 weekly observed CCGRBs. In this research, we examine the impact of these lockdowns on mental health and the varying success of government interventions in mitigating the pandemic's psychological effects. A longitudinal survey conducted in China during the pandemic revealed significant increases in anxiety, depression, and sleep disorders among the population. However, the effectiveness of lockdown, lockdown duration, and personal attributes in reducing these mental health issues was not consistently significant. This study's findings indicate that individuals subject to lockdown and those who have experienced longer lockdowns may exhibit similar levels of anxiety, depression, and sleep disorders. Additionally, this research reveals that certain personal attributes lose their initial negative effects as the lockdown period prolongs. In areas under strict lockdown, the initial increase in anxiety and depression disappeared after two weeks, while in areas under relaxed lockdown rules, the initial increase in anxiety and depression occurred after one week. This research's conclusions can be utilized to create more tailored mental health support services during similar public health crises.

learning has become a significant research area in the field of machine learning, with the goal of enhancing model performance by training on multiple tasks simultaneously. Recent studies have demonstrated the benefits of multi-tasking learning in a lifelong learning setting, where the goal is to accumulate new tasks without retraining. While existing work primarily focuses on learning single-type models, our study explores a real-world scenario that involves both learning from labeled data and learning from unlabeled data, with a diverse set of image classification tasks. To address this complex problem, we developed a Multi-Task Lifelong Learning framework that combines both supervised and unsupervised learning, allowing for the discovery of a limited number of shared task groups. The framework utilizes a network that comprises an encoder and a compact task descriptor, where the encoder shares a single set of feature maps across all tasks, and the task descriptor learns a binary code for each task. By learning from both labeled and unlabeled data, we applied a dual-optimization technique that separates the latent variables from the explicit task codes. The proposed method was evaluated on a diverse real-world dataset, known as Large Vision 2, which consists of 264 categories, with impressive results that outperformed the current state-of-the-art methods by a 3.7\% gap.

However, applying this approach has been impractically challenging for deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) due to an excessively large number of weights. This paper proposes an alternative measure of complexity that takes into account the structural organization of layers in DCNNs. Specifically, it proposes splitting the network into 'layer units' to calculate the sum of norms within each layer separately. This layer-based approach significantly reduces the number of weights to be managed and allows for more effective optimization processes. They defined a more limited type of structure, where each subset of siblings is independent, using the name "independent ordered trees" (IOTs). For IOTs with low levels of sibling independence, they provided quasipolynomial-time classification, but left the general case of high sibling independence unresolved. The theory of metric spaces has been extensively studied in its current form since the early 20th century and is now an established branch of mathematics with extensive applications. This paper explores the potential of replacing the standard distance function in metric spaces with a broader class of functions that satisfy specific discontinuity properties. Specifically, the paper investigates metric spaces whose underlying distance function exhibits continuity in approximate terms, a concept first introduced by A. Rajkov in 1957. It is demonstrated in this paper that these spaces are homeomorphic to certain types of classical metric spaces, providing a useful tool for solving fixed point problems and fixed point theorems in a broader context.

colliders like the Future Circular Collider (FCC) and the Compact Linear Collider (CLIC) will significantly advance our understanding of particle physics. As these machines approach the multitechnology frontier, researchers will be confronted with an overwhelming amount of data containing irrelevant information that could mask essential discoveries. As a result, developing efficient methods for data reduction and analysis becomes a critical aspect of the research process. In this work, we introduce a novel technique, the direct application of a two-step clustering method, to effectively compress event data. By first grouping similar clusters using a method like CTA or PTA, and then identifying the most characteristic events within each cluster, we can represent the entire data set with a much more compact set of events. In addition, we propose an alternative two-step method, combining a hierarchical clustering algorithm with an integrated density estimation algorithm. Both methods demonstrate excellent performance in reducing data, resulting in over 10 times fewer events with only a 0.1% decrease in accuracy.

The universe's dynamics can be effectively modeled using a multicomponent cosmological system, where multiple fluids interact with each other in a nonlinear and dynamic process. This situation is analogous to a complex electrical network with multiple components that can be represented using the Kirchhoff matrix. By applying the Kirchhoff matrix, we can examine the universe's dynamics during both the relativistic and nonrelativistic eras. Specifically, we investigate the impact of a multicomponent fluid on the scalar gravitational-wave background in the early universe. This involves solving a multicomponent bulk viscous model, where we can determine the exact expression for the energy density and polarization modes of the scalar gravitational-wave background. We also introduce a new statistical method to calculate the polarization modes of the scalar gravitational-wave background. This method allows us to determine the polarization modes of the scalar gravitational-wave background in both the relativistic and nonrelativistic eras. We can then apply this information to constrain the equation of state of multicomponent fluids using gravitational-wave background spectra.

High-quality, vast datasets are often produced by hiring multiple annotators to label the same data samples, a process known as dual-annotation. In real-world scenarios, annotators may produce errors or provide varying levels of quality, potentially wasting money and resources if not managed effectively. To address this challenge, we present a new model called the Dual-Annotation Network (DAN-Net), a probabilistic neural network that learns to prioritize annotated samples, allocate modeling resources based on the confidence of annotated labels, and integrate the provided labels in an efficient manner. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach over the current state of the art.

In a real-world scenario, V2G vehicles would likely operate under varying charging and emptying schedules, influenced by individual user needs and any relevant incentives or constraints. This study explores the behavior of V2G vehicles in relation to their state of charge and whether they are being charged or discharged. The resulting patterns of V2G behavior are then analyzed in order to estimate the overall proactive V2G capacity available to the power network. This study is based on a large dataset of real-world vehicle trips, and employs a statistical approach to model V2G behavior. The findings indicate that the distribution of V2G charging and discharging sessions follows a non-uniform pattern throughout the day, with distinct peaks occurring at specific hours. The data also reveals significant correlations between the levels of charging and discharging across different time periods. In order to facilitate seamless interaction between the V2G system and the power network, a scheduling mechanism is proposed that can match the available proactive V2G capacity with network requirements in real-time.

neural network-based robots in simulation is examined in relation to the acquisition of skills. The research suggests that educating these robots using reinforcement learning algorithms causes a significant discrepancy in performance, emerging from the disparity between how they behave in simulation and real-world settings. The underlying issue, it is proposed, stems from the fact that these methods prioritize optimizing the target task rather than developing a sense of physical intuition. As evidence, we observe that similar disruptions occur when the environment is altered, even if the changes affect the visual input. In order to address this problem, we suggest a solution based on the principle that a more robust learning algorithm should be able to generalize easily, even when the environment changes. As such, we propose an iterative process of training, where the robot is first taught to navigate its surroundings through trial and error, and then fine-tuned to perform specific tasks. The results of our experiments confirm that this method produces better performance that is more resistant to disruptions, as long as the changes do not affect the visual input, in which case the problem becomes the same as supervised learning.

ann Hypothesis (RH) has an immense significance in the field of number theory, and its association with the distribution of prime numbers is well established. The RH has been confirmed for a considerable set of prime numbers through various methods, including those employing holomorphic modular forms and motivic Galois groups. In contrast, the RH's connection to quadratic forms has only recently been explored. Just as the RH informs us about the prime number distribution, its extension to a set of prime numbers determined by quadratic forms should reveal the distribution of those primes. The aim of this study is to link the RH to the distribution of primes within a quadratic field by applying a novel combination of class field theory and Fourier analysis. The resulting connection leads to the hypothesis that the density of primes, whose prime factors generate a specified class in a quadratic field, can be determined by the Fourier transform of a specific function. This study also proposes several concrete densities that can be decided by this hypothesis. The proposed strategy can be applied to any prime number distributing according to a specific quadratic form, allowing us to formulate numerous conjectures of this kind. The study shows that one such conjecture implies the generalization of the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture for elliptic curves defined over certain quadratic fields.

dynamically assembled human crowds, when walking, behave as a uniform and seamless whole. Conversely, recent findings indicate that integrating individual human walkers into a crowd results in an opaque and irreducible collective dynamics. This study bridges this gap by examining the differences between discrete and continuous representations of walking crowds. We demonstrate that a simple and precise discrete-model architecture, comprising single agents guided by local rules, successfully replicates the intricate patterns of crowd circulation observed in continuous models. This successful replication holds true even in complex scenarios involving on-ramp entries and exit points along a walking path. We analyze our results mathematically and numerically, proving that a discrete crowd exhibits nearly infinite correlation across the crowd body. This level of correlation serves as a critical component in producing the smooth, uninterrupted flow of walking observed in our simulations.

(LISA) will provide precise measurements of gravitational waves in the frequency range of 0.001-0.1 Hz. Analyzing the timing of cosmic vacuum decay using LISA data offers potential to detect this process. The associated waveform features a unique pattern in the power spectral density at ~10^-21 Hz^(-1) strength. Accounting for the impact of various astrophysical and cosmological factors, including supernovae and the cosmic 61 Cygni system, is crucial in this research. These factors contribute an extra ~10^-20 Hz^(-1) to the power spectral density. As a result, identifying the cosmic vacuum decay signal with LISA will be significantly more challenging than detecting other gravitational waves. Additionally, this research reveals that the cosmic 61 Cygni system, with its slightly uneven orbital period, may obscure the cosmic vacuum decay signal by as much as 10 times in certain frequencies. However, thanks to LISA's high measurement precision, it will be able to eliminate these sources of noise and reveal the cosmic vacuum decay. Furthermore, this research introduces a new method for estimating the (E/ c^2) value associated with cosmic 61 Cygni, which will be determined with an accuracy of 0.01 upon observing this system with LISA.

By gradually reducing the height of this barrier, while maintaining its impenetrability, we cause the 'quasiparticle pair' to bind together and form a single anyon carrying symmetry charge q, thus achieving an anyon condensate of this single anyon type, with the charge value being a secondary characteristic. 's theory of general relativity is a highly relevant topic in the field of theoretical astrophysics. Several deviations from general relativity have been proposed over the years, primarily aimed at addressing the theory's implicit assumptions. Conformal general relativity is one such deviation, formulated by varying the theory's action under a conformal transformation while keeping the conformal factor's Ricci scalar coefficient constant. This paper delves into the analysis of conformal general relativity within the framework of the de Sitter universe, specifically focusing on the conformal vanishing Ricci scalar theory. The proposed model is mathematically represented by the equation $\bar{\rho}(R-4\Lambda) = k \bar{\rho}^2$, where $\bar{\rho}$ represents the conformal density, $R$ is the Ricci curvature scalar, $\Lambda$ is the cosmological constant, and $k$ is a constant. By solving this equation, we derive non-singular de Sitter spacetime solutions for both the conformal vanishing Ricci scalar theory and the vanishing Ricci scalar theory under specific constraints on the conformal density function. Additionally, we demonstrate that the conformal vanishing Ricci scalar theory exhibits power-law de Sitter spacetime solutions for a specific value of the conformal density function's coefficient.

isy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices, are hindered by programming limitations due to their small number of qubits. One of the most effective methods for mitigating this constraint is Quantum Error Mitigation (QEM). Realizing its full potential, however, depends on balancing the reduction of error introduced by qubit usage with the complexity of implementing that reduction. In this research, we analyze the trade-offs involved with one popular QEM technique, Quantum Fault Tolerant compiling (QFTC), in relation to one of the most widely accepted metrics for error reduction, the 2q-circuit Pauli weight. Our findings indicate that QFTC, when applied to this specific error reduction metric, results in an increase directly proportional to the square of the number of qubits used in the original circuit, for circuits consisting of two-qubit operations that are uniformly independent. Furthermore, we propose an extension to QFTC that reduces the error increase, and demonstrate its effectiveness with the 2q-circuit Pauli weight, especially for large, two-qubit circuits commonly found in NISQ programs.

Despite the potential benefits for applications in data, the mixed-derivative operator based bilinear map between two Riemannian manifolds has not been extensively explored as a learning tool.  We establish that a particular operator, the double-Cascades operator, which utilizes the mixed-derivative operator and is based on the manifold version of the Hodge star, can be used to learn mapping between two Riemannian manifolds.  By leveraging the Hodge decomposition and the Poincare-Hodge theorem, we demonstrate that the operator is surjective when the manifolds satisfy certain conditions, which enables us to prove that it is also stable. We then compare the algorithm to previous ones and show that it has an analytical form, which greatly reduces the number of parameters needed.  We test the algorithm with synthetic and real data, which shows that it produces accurate and efficient results.

This result holds whether the demon distinguishes between different velocity ranges or separates molecules with different velocities. This conclusion is reached through a detailed examination of the demon's operation, including its velocity measurement process, and does not presume any particular thermodynamic relations.  Consequently, our findings contribute to the proof of the impossibility of constructing a perpetual motion machine in a closed system, by highlighting the inherent generation of entropy within such a machine.

In this work, we propose a new method called indirect testing, which involves presenting the AI with two groups of words: those that describe a visual scene and those that describe a character's actions.  The AI then has to use these two sets of words to accurately predict a character's emotions.  If the AI performs well on this task, we test its ability to understand the relationships between words by presenting it with new sets of words, both visual and descriptive of character actions.  Our results show that our method works effectively and can be used to guide the training of more efficient AI models.

One promising approach in natural language processing involves the use of graph neural networks, which have shown excellence in identifying complex patterns in data structured as graphs.  Building on previous research using graph neural networks for offensiveness detection, this paper presents several innovative modifications designed to enhance performance and versatility. As energy consumption poses challenges to the deployment of centralized CRANs, a novel architecture has emerged based on edge computing, referred to as the Energy-Aware Virtualized RAN (EA-VRAN). This edge computing architecture has implications for the energy consumption of RANs and has not been thoroughly explored in the literature. This paper formalizes the EA-VRAN architecture and delves into analyzing its energy characteristics from both a mobile device's and a cloud provider's perspective. This proposed method is applied to an EA-VRAN mobile edge computing environment and demonstrates that energy efficiency can be effectively improved through optimization.

We then employ this revised principle to prove that the entanglement of scattered particles results from the invariance of specific properties, such as momentum, particularly when considering weak and discrete variations. the atomic level is the central goal of theoretical materials science.  First-principles methods, specifically DFT and GMACS, are highly effective for this purpose.  However, these methods have distinct characteristics and advantages.  DFT is an established and versatile approach with numerous applications, whereas GMACS is relatively new and needs more practical applications.  Both methods can model materials using atomic coordinates and occupation matrices, so we've developed a way to link their results and use the differences to quantify an 'effective temperature' in materials.  This concept is demonstrated across multiple DFT and GMACS studies, and further developed into a metric that assesses the coherence of a system and indicates potential gaps in the energy spectrum.  This idea can be applied to any first-principles model and opens up new avenues for analyzing and understanding quantum many-body systems.

The cylinder's inner surface is non-wetting, while the outer surface is wetting, with the fluid flowing in a laminar fashion. The flow pattern in this scenario is known to be symmetrical and axisymmetric. The outer layer's wetting surface causes the formation of a thin boundary layer there, as well as a larger, more stable laminar flow region further out. The size of the boundary layer layer, however, is determined by the flow's interaction with the inner surface. The effect of the inner surface on this phenomenon leads to two possible boundary layer sizes, resulting in the creation of a unique recirculation bubble that forms at the intersection of these two layers and is influenced by the flow from the inner surface. The size of this bubble will be expressed in terms of an important dimensionless group created by combining relevant parameters, specifically the Reynolds and Peclet numbers, as well as the ratios of the inner and outer layer lengths to the cylinder's overall length.

The calculations enable the quantification of the second-harmonic generation (SHG) effect in this material and the assessment of its potential for applications requiring large optical nonlinearity. In this research, we examine the role of language structure in expressing the meaning of sentences. A key aspect of this is the sequence-to-sequence model, which has become a fundamental framework for translating and generating text. By analyzing the underlying syntax and semantics of language with these models, we can improve their performance and ensure they produce coherent and realistic text. In this paper, we outline an approach using a sequence-to-sequence model, specifically one that incorporates neural networks, for generating natural language from a given meaning representation. By applying this method to a sequence-to-sequence translator for Natural Logic, we demonstrate a significant enhancement in both coherence and realism of generated text.

Most CL methods are designed with a focus on balancing tasks by minimizing forgetting and adjusting the neural network.  However, few studies thoroughly examine the strategy of task selection in continuous learning from streams of tasks.  We propose Category Preservation (CP), a principle that selectively chooses tasks to learn from based on the category of tasks the network has already learned from. of the antiferromagnet $\alpha$ -LiFeAs, characterized by their magnetic behavior under applied pressure and temperature.  A significant observation made in this study indicates that the Néel temperature, which marks the point at which an antiferromagnet loses its ordering, can be consistently elevated through the application of increasing pressure.  Notably, this Néel temperature can be brought above room temperatures, a first in the $\alpha$ -LiFeAs series of compounds.  In addition to this finding, the magnetic susceptibility of these crystals was found to display an unexpected behavior at low temperatures and high magnetic fields, following a Curie law rather than the anticipated paramagnetic behavior.  The occurrence of this behavior is attributed to the presence of free Fe$^{2+}$ ions within the crystal lattice.  In order to gain a deeper theoretical understanding of these phenomena, our data was analyzed within the framework of the Zinn-Andrean model, which suggests that the presence of these free Fe$^{2+}$ ions may result in the localization of adjacent spin waves due to their overlap within the same energy range.  Consequently, this over-crowding of energy bands may contribute to the increased occurrence of these free Fe$^{2+}$ ions, and potentially other similar instances, at higher temperatures and under greater magnetic fields.

As a consequence, the risk of a critical wireless infrastructure failure resulting in catastrophic societal consequences also increases.  To address this vulnerability, a proposed methodology leverages machine learning and network virtualization to create redundant, fault-tolerant virtual networks for critical wireless infrastructure.  By training a classifier to recognize patterns in real-time network data and predict potential failures, the system can automatically reconfigure the virtual network to minimize downtime. the primate brain has been hindered by the complex and multi-scale nature of its cortical connections.  While studies of the cerebral cortex have revealed distinct functional areas within each brain region across different levels of activity, a similar distinction has not been drawn for the structural connectivity of the brain.  To address this, researchers have employed techniques that combine multi-scale methods with statistical analysis to identify regions within the cerebral cortex that are distinct based on their structural connectivity patterns.  These studies have pinpointed locations and shapes of specific regional structures throughout the brain, identifying areas such as the lateral occipital complex, the lateral posterior region, and the medial orbital region.  The thickness of these regions, which vary in different areas of the brain, was found to be correlated with the surface area of the cortex they occupy, and the gray matter density within these regions was found to be uniformly consistent, indicating a uniform regional structure across the brain.  The shape and location of these regions were found to be highly consistent across different primate species, although the cortex-to-white matter ratio was found to be a key factor in defining them.

observed in protoplanetary discs can be explained by a phenomenon called the 'dead zone', where a sudden and extreme slowdown of gas flow within a specific region of the disc causes it to become 'frozen' and inhibit further accretion. To investigate this, we ran computer simulations that modeled the 'dead zone' phenomenon and studied its effects on the flow of gas within the disc. Our findings reveal that the 'dead zone' can become 'frozen' due to an irreversible decrease in flow velocity, and that this 'frozen' area can persist over a long period of time. Furthermore, we found that the 'dead zone' can be located at any distance from the star, and that it can also vary in size. Our results also show that the 'dead zone' can only be overcome when the flow of gas is triggered by a sudden disturbance, such as a protoplanetary object. If this hypothesis is correct, it could provide an explanation for the slow accretion rates and large sizes of giant planets that form in these discs.

The underlying theory is an extended version of the Standard Model, specifically the 'b c ∅' scenario, which incorporates a pair of vector or axial-vector 'b c ∅' bosons. These bosons interact with the three lepton flavours in a different manner and contribute to several processes that display LFNU. In the 'b c ∅' scenario the LFNU effect is primarily attributed to the 'b c ∅' couplings with the leptons, which significantly deviate from the predictions of the Standard Model. This study expands on this research by examining the ability to predict the semantic categories of a newly presented auditory sentence. For the experiment, 20 experts created category labels for 1000 sentences from the word dataset, which were then used to train a new classifier. When the entire BERT network was applied to an auditory sentence, a strong semantic category representation was generated at a rate of 77%. for evaluating the effectiveness of FRL in tackling the aforementioned
challenges. The CERES framework is unique in that it categorizes multi-agent
scenarios based on the relationship between agents and the similarity of each
agent's data, thereby enabling the efficient design of an FRL system. Furthermore,
we demonstrate the capabilities of this framework through a comprehensive
evaluation of two scenarios, and the results show that our approach achieves
better performance compared to both MARL and traditional reinforcement learning

Existing methods often result in clothing that appears unnatural, requires an unrealistic number of vertices, and is inefficient to render.  To address these issues, we introduce a novel approach utilizing implicit surfaces to represent both human avatars and clothing.  By utilizing a single-point sampling operation to generate mesh data and adhering to physics, our method produces realistic and naturally-positioned clothing on avatars, even when scanned or predicted using simple and lightweight representations.  We also introduce an implicit refinement technique that enhances the appearance of clothing and simplifies rendering.  Our method is particularly effective for rendering scenes in video games and similar high-performance graphics applications, and we demonstrate our approach by applying it to real and predicted avatar datasets.

To understand their common characteristics and individual differences, this study comprehensively reviews 25 contact tracing apps implemented on Linux systems, specifically focusing on Raspberry Pi devices running Raspbian. During the research, it became clear that many countries have their own customized contact tracing solutions, often employing distinct techniques. Some popular methods include using Bluetooth Low Energy for proximity detection, generating unique identifiers, and relying on centralized or decentralized databases. This review also highlights several potential security concerns associated with these apps, including the risk of identifier interception and the potential for unauthorized access to database management systems. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that many of these apps lack essential features like notification configuration and logout functionality. This review can serve as a valuable resource for developers working on contact tracing projects, enabling them to leverage established solutions and address existing pain points in app development.

This study focuses on a specific scenario where the Hamiltonian has a SU(3) symmetry and the scattering data satisfy certain equations derived from the mathematical framework of three-body systems with symmetric interactions.  By combining analytical and numerical methods, we aim to explore whether the Hamiltonian can be reliably reconstructed from the scattering equations with particular initial conditions, specifically those representing soft interactions.  Our analysis involves directly solving the scattering equations and examining the properties of the reconstructed potential energy.  We also utilized the three-body parameter, a, in our calculations.  Our results show that the reconstructed potential energy matches the original, symmetric potential energy when the parameter a is negative or zero, but differs when a is positive.  However, in the latter case, we found that the Hamiltonian can still be accurately reconstructed under certain conditions, specifically, low energy levels or large negative values of a.  Our study provides valuable insights into the inverse problem in quantum mechanics and has implications for future research, also giving us an idea that in some cases where the three-body parameter is positive the inverse problem can be solvable.

We examine how the one-shot snowdrift game cooperation levels behave under different levels of punishment in a group of uniformly random strategy selecting agents in a large population. We provide an explicit expression for the equilibrium cooperation probability in the one-shot snowdrift game, which we find to be the inverse of the punishment level multiplied by the snowdrift game cooperation threshold, where the threshold is a value between 0 and 1 that depends on the payoff parameters and the punishment level. We verify the validity of our expression by comparing it to the cooperation levels obtained from simulations. finite temperatures have been extensively studied in recent years, and we've seen a significant amount of evidence for their existence.  This research investigates the fundamental characteristics of such warm phases, and particularly, we focus on a specific protocol known as the "quenching" process.  When we rapidly change temperature in this way, the system eventually settles into a specific warm phase, and we found that the quenching method plays a crucial role in mapping the system's entire parameter space.  We utilized this method to study a simplified model that incorporates a high-density state and a warm version of a topologically-ordered phase, and we were able to visualize the system's behavior across its entire parameter space.  During the quenching process, we observed that the system's dynamics can be broken down into two distinct periods: an initial brief episode of chaos, followed by an enduring warm phase that closely resembles the system's equilibrium behavior.  We further discovered that this warm phase exhibits many characteristics found in systems that have been cooled to extremely low temperatures, and it can even support unique, fragile states that are unstable in systems that are cooled slowly.  This research provides a comprehensive overview of the system's behavior during the quenching process, and it reveals that the system's topology remains intact regardless of the rate at which the temperature is changed.

machine learning model is trained to classify data that has been deliberately misleadingly labeled by specifying the predicted probabilities of each label. This research focuses on linear and logistic regression, neural network regression with a logistic loss function, and nearest neighbors methods. Our analysis reveals that these algorithms are highly susceptible to manipulation, especially when the training data includes labels that are relatively common and well-defined. This vulnerability can lead to inaccurate predictions and a significant decrease in the performance of the model, even when the training data constitutes a large random sample. This issue is particularly concerning for machine learning systems that are widely trusted and are therefore more likely to be compromised by fraudulent labeling. This research highlights the importance of verifying the legitimacy of training data, especially when it has been collected by other parties. Furthermore, it proposes an alternative approach to labeling data based on the validation of model performance rather than relying on unreliable labels. This new labeling method can be used in conjunction with the machine learning algorithms examined in this research.

Previous research has utilized five-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations to study this process in low-mass stars and found that quasi-periodic oscillations occur in these systems due to a specific mechanism.  Those oscillations result from a growing current loop buried within the star's interior breaking free from magnetic reconnection resistance and becoming unstabilized as it rises.  A separate, related loop then becomes unstable and the cycle repeats.  We've run similar simulations on more massive stars and discovered that their activity cycles involve a deeper, persistently rotating magnetic field within the star's interior.  However, even on low-mass stars, this inner field is only visible beneath very weak surface magnetic fields.  Those surface fields are what break through to observe the star's spotty surface.  The deep field's persistence suggests a possible pathway for enhanced, ultra-strong magnetic field activity ultimately giving rise to these stars.

an index case is a critical parameter in continental-scale epidemic modeling, yet its average value varies significantly across real-world data sets despite having a similar underlying structure.  We propose a novel statistical approach to establish a consistent relationship between this average value and the parameters of a weighted degree-based SIS network model.  Specifically, we establish that the expected number of secondary infections per index case is proportional to the product of the global epidemic parameter and the variance of a degree distribution, provided certain mixing conditions are met.  Building on this discovery, we develop a weighted degree-based target immunization strategy that minimizes the final epidemic size by prioritizing nodes with the highest variance in degree.  Our method achieves superior results compared to multiple benchmark strategies in a wide range of network scenarios.

By analyzing a comprehensive set of discrete symmetries - including those affecting the right-handed neutrinos and the scalar potential - we identify the most effective strategies for eliminating the problematic lightest Higgs mass contribution. Our investigation reveals that incorporating the top-quark and bottom-quark Yukawa couplings into the discrete symmetries can successfully avoid all unwanted scalar particle masses, whereas including the $\mu$-term leads to only a limited solution set. To illustrate the cosmological implications, we integrate the WIMP inductive dark matter scenario into the model, finding that the most viable solutions result in Higgs mass around 125 GeV, in alignment with experimental data.

common English idiom used to contrast two extreme situations. Research on this idiom has focused on its grammatical aspects, neglecting its capacity to create a vivid image in the mind of the listener/reader. This paper rekindles interest in this idiom, exploring its fundamental components - "night" and "day" - as well as the relationship between them. In the process, we delve into the broader context of English proverbs and sayings, examining how they convey meaningful insights in a memorable way. Through an analysis of "night" and "day", we discover how these fundamental elements of the human experience are often juxtaposed in English literature to highlight the inherent oppositeness present within them. Ultimately, we propose that "like night and day" embodies the complex yet inherent contrast inherent within the human world, making it a compelling topic for further linguistic and philosophical exploration.

Existing methods for comparing data typically involve automatic or semi-automatic processes, using similarities in visual appearance or text-based characteristics, but these may not be sufficient for distinguishing between new and established categories if they fail to capture more fundamental underlying attributes.  Taking this into consideration, our research introduces a novel approach called Discovery Learning from Observations, taking advantage of a closely related body of work known as the rubber chicken hypothesis, which suggests that the most distinguishing features of a category are those that are consistently challenged by counterexamples.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through a series of experiments using the CLEVR-Adv dataset, generating new data samples from existing categories and verifying that they possess the same attributes as the original data.  Our results show that models trained on the existing categories are able to accurately classify the new data samples, while models trained on the new data samples are able to accurately classify the original data.  We also observe that the new data samples have similar complexity and coverage to the original data.  Additionally, we find that the new data samples are diverse and distinct from each other.  We compare our method to several alternative approaches, including human labelers, and find that our method produces high-quality new data samples that are comparable to those of human labelers.  We also discuss the implications of our work for machine learning and data evaluation.

Neural Network-Based Hydroacoustic Classification Networks.  When implementing spatial pooling on spectrogram data, a standard approach assumes a fixed low-frequency cut-off when performing an exponential moving average.  However, the effects of varying this frequency cut-off and the pooling method itself have not been systematically analyzed in the field of marine bio-acoustics.  In this research, six different low-frequency cut-off values and three distinct pooling layers were tested on a classification network using a 10-frequency band spectrogram dataset obtained from NOAA.  Comparing the average classification accuracy across all tests revealed that a specific combination of a fixed low-frequency cut-off and a sum pooling layer yields the highest average classification accuracy.  However, in scenarios where data sets with varying frequency bands are present, implementing a dynamic low-frequency cut-off or a weighted sum pooling layer may lead to enhanced performance.
